*Owlet Cares is our advocacy initiative that is dedicated to making a positive impact in the lives of babies and parents. One way we do this is by partnering with community-led groups from all over the world who share our mission.*


*Each month, we shine a spotlight on one of our foundation partners and the important work they are doing. This month, we’d like to introduce you to Nicole Thorfinnson of Dear NICU Mama, - a nonprofit organization that aims to bring hope and connection to past and present parents of NICU babies, through a community where mothers and families feel seen, understood, and supported.*


*The quotes, stories, and experiences included here are those of the individuals and are not representative of Owlet’s views or claims about our product. Dear NICU Mama, is an Owlet Cares partner and receives a 3-for-1 product match from Owlet. Nicole serves on the Board of Directors of Dear NICU Mama, and was not paid for this post. *****


*If you have questions about your health or your child’s health, please seek guidance from a qualified healthcare provider or mental health professional.*


**By: Nicole Thorfinnson**


Before becoming a mom, I had heard of Owlet Dream Sock®. I knew the basics of what it did and how it worked, but I never gave much thought to whether I would actually use one of the monitors myself.


And then I had a premature baby.


My daughter was born at 33 weeks and spent 46 days in the NICU. For those 46 days, monitors were simply part of our everyday life. She was constantly hooked up to machines tracking her heart rate, oxygen levels and more. I knew her numbers. I watched them rise and fall. And, more than once, I watched those monitors alert us when she stopped breathing.


As terrifying as those moments were, there was also comfort in knowing someone, or something, was always watching.


Then came the day we had waited so long for:


we got to bring her home.


I wanted so badly to live in the world of trusting that she was fine. We had been cleared to leave the hospital. She was ready. I should have been able to breathe a sigh of relief.


Instead, my anxiety was overwhelming.


I barely slept once we got home. Every noise, every movement and every moment of silence made me wonder if she was okay.


For 46 days, the only version of motherhood I had known involved knowing my baby's pulse rate and oxygen levels. I had spent weeks next to monitors, watching numbers and trusting alarms to let us know when something wasn't right.


The numbers weren't new to me. Not having them was.


Going home and suddenly having none of that felt incredibly jarring.


After one sleepless night, we went to Target and


bought a Dream Sock


. It ended up being one of the best things we did for our family.


For the first time since bringing my daughter home, I felt like I could sleep. Knowing she was being monitored gave me a sense of peace that I desperately needed during that transition.


If you've ever watched your baby struggle to breathe


, whether because of silent reflux or for reasons you don't fully understand, you know how terrifying that experience can be. Once you've seen it happen, simply telling yourself, “


She's fine. She's sleeping. Everything is okay”,


isn't always enough to quiet


your brain.


For me, using Dream Sock wasn't about obsessing over every number. It gave me enough peace of mind to finally rest.


And I know I'm not alone in that feeling.


I've talked with many other NICU moms who have described how difficult it is to go from a world where you know


every number


to suddenly knowing


nothing


. One day, your baby's vitals are displayed on a screen 24/7. The next, you're home, staring into a bassinet and being asked to trust that everything is okay.


It's a reality shift that's difficult to understand until you've experienced it.


For our family, Dream Sock became a bridge between those two worlds.


While the Dream Sock doesn't replace hospital monitoring, it helped me slowly move from the constant monitoring


of the NICU to the normalcy we had worked so hard to reach at home. It didn't erase the anxiety that came with our NICU experience, but it gave me enough peace of mind to sleep, breathe and begin trusting that we really were okay.


And after 46 days of waiting to bring my baby home, that peace of mind meant everything.


**Author Bio:**


Nicole Thorfinnson is a marketing leader, wife, sister, daughter, and mom driven by the power of human connection. She believes community often begins close to home but can extend far beyond it through shared experiences, vulnerability, and a collective desire to leave things better for those who come after. Professionally, Nicole serves as the Director of Marketing at Advanced Business Methods (ABM), where she focuses on aligning strategy, storytelling, and meaningful connection. She is passionate about casting vision and creating clear, actionable pathways to bring that vision to life. Nicole is also a NICU mom—an experience that profoundly shaped her perspective on empathy, resilience, and advocacy. Giving back to the NICU community is deeply personal to her, and she is passionate about paying forward the support and encouragement her family once received. She is honored to serve on the Board of Directors for Dear NICU Mama, where she supports families with compassion, encouragement, and connection—both in the NICU and beyond.


*If your baby spent time in the NICU or has any health conditions, talk with your baby’s doctor about whether Dream Sock is right for your baby. Dream Sock is intended for healthy babies 1–18 months old weighing 6–30 lbs, and is not intended for babies diagnosed with heart or breathing conditions.*


*Dream Sock® is intended to track baby's pulse rate and oxygen level and keep parents informed. Dream Sock is not intended to diagnose, treat or cure any disease or other condition, including but not limited to, Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS) and/or Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV). Medical decisions should never be made solely using Dream Duo™ and Dream Sock data. Dream Duo and Dream Sock should not substitute for the care and oversight of an adult or consultation with medical professionals.*
